"Sacked" as an adjective has two distinct meanings depending on the context. Both come from the verb "to sack," but they describe completely different situations.

This is the most everyday, modern use of the word.

When a person has been told to leave their job by their employer — against their own wish — they can be described as "sacked."

"The sacked employees stood outside the factory gate."
"The sacked minister gave a press conference defending himself."
"A group of sacked workers filed a legal case against the company."

Here, "sacked" tells you that the person did not resign voluntarily. Someone in power — a boss, a board, an authority — made the decision to remove them from their position.

Tone and feel: The word is blunt and direct. It carries a slightly harsh edge — more forceful than saying "dismissed" or "let go." In newspapers, headlines, and everyday speech, "sacked" grabs attention. Compare:

  • "The fired coach..." — neutral, common in American English
  • "The dismissed officer..." — formal and official
  • "The sacked coach..." — punchy, slightly dramatic; very common in British, Australian, and Indian English

What it doesn't tell you on its own is why the person was sacked. It could be because of wrongdoing, poor performance, company downsizing, political disagreement, or any other reason. The surrounding context usually makes that clear.

This is the older, more historical meaning of the word, and it applies to places — cities, towns, villages, temples — not to people.

When an invading army or group attacks a place, loots its wealth, destroys its buildings, and harms its people, that place is described as "sacked."

"The sacked city was left with nothing but ashes and rubble."
"Refugees fled from the sacked villages along the border."
"The sacked temple had been stripped of all its gold."

This sense paints a picture of total devastation — not just theft, but widespread destruction, violence, and chaos. It is a word associated with wars, conquests, and invasions throughout history.

Tone and feel: This meaning is more dramatic and literary. You'll encounter it in history books, journalism about war, and fiction. It is heavier and more vivid than simply saying "looted" or "attacked." A "sacked city" wasn't just robbed — it was overwhelmed and ravaged.
How to Tell Which Meaning Is Intended

This is simple once you notice what the word is describing:

  • If "sacked" describes a person (a worker, an official, a manager), it means fired from their job.
  • If "sacked" describes a place (a city, town, village, temple), it means violently plundered and destroyed.

The two meanings almost never cause confusion because they attach to completely different kinds of subjects.
The Underlying Idea in Both Cases

Interestingly, both meanings share a common thread: something has been taken away by force. In one case, a person's livelihood and position have been forcibly removed. In the other, a place's wealth and peace have been forcibly stripped away. The adjective "sacked" in both cases describes something that was once whole and secure, now broken by an external force.

1. "Sacked" implies passivity.
The sacked person or place did not choose what happened to them. This is why it's called an adjective form of the past participle — it describes a state that was done to someone or something. A "sacked employee" is someone something was done to, not someone who acted.

2. In everyday speech, Meaning 1 is far more common.
If you hear or read "sacked" in a news article, a conversation, or a TV show today, it almost certainly refers to someone losing their job. The historical/war meaning (Meaning 2) appears mostly in books, documentaries, or formal writing about conflicts and history.

3. "Sacked" (job loss) is especially dominant in British and Commonwealth English.
In American English, people more often say "fired." But in Britain, India, Australia, and many other countries, "sacked" is the go-to word.

4. The word applies to all levels of power.
You can say a factory worker was sacked, but equally, a prime minister, a general, or a CEO can be described as sacked. The word does not care about how high or low the position is — only that the removal was forced.

Describes a personDismissed from their job involuntarily
Describes a placeViolently looted and destroyed

In short: a sacked worker lost their job. A sacked city lost everything. Both were stripped of something by force.
